# Release & Hotfix Branch Rules

**Read this file in full before taking any action when `git branch --show-current` matches `release/*` or `hotfix/*`.** These rules apply *in addition to* the Hard Rules in [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md). On `feature/*` and `fix/*` branches they do not apply and this file can be ignored.

See the branch table in [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md) > Branch Rules for which branch merges where.

## Back-merge rules (GitFlow)

To prevent `develop` drifting from production:
- When a `release/*` branch is merged to `main` at go-live, it must also be merged back to `develop`.
- When a `hotfix/*` is merged to `main`, it must also be merged back to `develop`.
- When a `fix/release-*` is merged into its `release/*` parent and the release later ships, the forward-merge to `develop` happens as part of the release back-merge above — no separate action.

## Release Branch Behaviour

When on a `release/*` branch, the following rules apply in addition to all Hard Rules.

**Before writing any code, always:**
1. State a plan — which files will change, what will change in each, and why.
2. Assess blast radius — how many components, hooks, or pages consume each file being changed? Flag explicitly if any file has more than 3 consumers or is Tier 2 or above.
3. Wait for explicit developer confirmation before making any edit, including trivial ones.

**Allowed on release branches:**
- Read-only skills: `/generate-changelog`, `/pr-checklist`, `/code-quality`
- Trivial non-code changes (copy corrections, version bumps, feature flag toggles) — plan + confirm required
- Code logic fixes — only on a `fix/release-{version}_{description}` sub-branch, never directly on the release branch

**Not allowed on release branches:**
- New features or scope additions not in the release
- Refactoring
- Dependency changes
- Tier 1 or Tier 2 file changes without the same owner approval required on feature branches

**How to make a code fix on a release branch:**

The fix PR targets the release branch. Once the release ships, the fix flows into `develop` via the release back-merge — do not open a separate PR from `fix/release-*` to `develop`.

```bash
# Branch from the release branch — not from develop
```

Only **Dev** is continuously tied to `develop` (deploys on every merge) — that part is fine, it's meant to be the shared integration environment. But SIT/UAT/Stage/Prod are promoted by pointing a workflow at a **branch or tag ref** (`workflow_dispatch` with a `ref` input). In practice this breaks down two ways:

1. **PR branches don't survive.** Once a story's PR merges to `develop`, its branch is typically deleted. There's nothing left to point a later deploy at — you'd have to keep branches alive indefinitely just to remember what shipped where, which doesn't scale past a couple of people.
2. **Environments get forced into lockstep.** If Test, SIT, and UAT all deploy the *same* release branch as it exists right now, they can't run independent testing cycles — a fix landed for UAT is *also* now sitting on whatever branch Test/SIT were pointed at, even if those teams haven't finished their own pass yet.

The fix: promote immutable tags, not floating branches
------------------------------------------------------

This is standard GitFlow practice that's currently missing here: **when a batch of work is ready to test, tag it. Every environment deploys a specific tag, never "whatever's on a branch right now."**

* Tags are **immutable and permanent** — `v0.1.0-rc.1` always means exactly one commit, unlike a PR branch that gets deleted on merge.
* Each environment can sit on a **different tag at the same time** — Test can be validating `v0.2.0-rc.1` while SIT is still working through `v0.1.0-rc.3` and UAT is signing off `v0.1.0-rc.2`. That's what actually decouples the environments' cadences from each other.
* **No new tooling required.** Every `deploy-*.yml` workflow already takes a `ref` input via `workflow_dispatch`, and `git checkout` doesn't care whether `ref` is a branch name or a tag name. The gap today is process (nobody's cutting tags), not infrastructure.

Tag naming convention
---------------------

Matches this repo's existing `release/v{version}` branch convention (see `.docs/releaseBranchesRules.md`'s own `release/v0.1.0` example) and standard SemVer.

| Tag pattern | Meaning | Example | Points at | Who creates it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `vX.Y.Z-rc.<N>` | Release candidate — a stabilising snapshot, not yet final. Cheap to cut, iterate freely. | `v0.1.0-rc.1`, `v0.1.0-rc.2` | A commit on `release/vX.Y.Z` | Any developer |
| `vX.Y.Z` | Final release — the exact candidate that passed every gate. This is what actually promotes through UAT → Stage → Prod. | `v0.1.0` | The `release/vX.Y.Z` commit being merged to `main` | Release manager / tier-1-approver only |
| `vX.Y.Z-hotfix.<N>` | Emergency fix candidate, outside the normal release train | `v0.1.1-hotfix.1` | A commit on `hotfix/vX.Y.Z` | Release manager / tier-1-approver only |

**X.Y.Z meaning:** **X** (major) — breaking change or major milestone (e.g. a new region launch), rare. **Y** (minor) — new stories/features, the normal per-release bump. **Z** (patch) — bug-fix-only releases / hotfixes.

**Pre-launch: MAJOR starts at** `0`**.** SemVer explicitly reserves `0.y.z` for initial development ("anything MAY change at any time"), which fits this project's current phase exactly. Cut one release per sprint as a MINOR bump — sprint 1 is `v0.1.0`, sprint 2 is `v0.2.0`, and so on. PATCH within an already-cut sprint version still means bug-fix-only, same as post-launch. `v1.0.0` **is reserved for go-live** — the first time MAJOR moves off `0` — after which MAJOR reverts to its normal rare-breaking-change meaning.

### Anatomy of a tag — `v0.1.0-rc.2` broken down

| Part | Name | Meaning | Increments when... |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `v` | Prefix | Not a version number itself — a literal marker so the tag is unambiguously "a version" and `git tag -l 'v*'` filters cleanly. Not part of SemVer itself, but near-universal on git tags. | Never changes |
| `0` | **MAJOR** | Breaking change or major milestone. Locked at `0` pre-launch (see note above) — `1` at go-live, then rare thereafter. | At go-live (→1), then only for a new region launch, a checkout-flow replatform, or anything severe enough that every in-flight release branch would need to rebase against it |
| `1` | **MINOR** | A normal release — new stories/features, backward compatible | Every sprint, when a new `release/vX.Y.Z` branch is cut from `develop` |
| `0` | **PATCH** | Bug-fix-only release against an already-shipped MAJOR.MINOR | A hotfix after `v0.1.0` has already shipped → the next one is `v0.1.1`, not a new minor |
| `-rc.2` | **Pre-release identifier** | "Release candidate" — this specific build is being validated, not yet final. The number is a simple incrementing counter, not an environment reference. | Each time a fix lands and a new candidate build is cut for the same target version |

The `-rc` number does **not** correspond to an environment — the same `v0.1.0-rc.1` tag can be deployed to Test today and SIT tomorrow. Which environment tested which candidate is tracked via each `deploy-*.yml`'s GitHub Actions run history, not the tag name. The only other pre-release suffix in this scheme is `-hotfix.<N>` (same pattern, cut from `hotfix/vX.Y.Z` instead of `release/vX.Y.Z`). No suffix at all (plain `vX.Y.Z`) means final, shipped.

**Why the dot before the number (**`-rc.2`**, not** `-rc2`**):** SemVer pre-release identifiers compare numerically only when they're separate dot-separated fields. `rc.10` and `rc.2` compare correctly as numbers (10 > 2). `rc10` and `rc2` compare as one string each and sort alphabetically — `rc10` would incorrectly sort *before* `rc2`. This matters directly for the safe-upward-deploy check below.

The Test gate
-------------

Decided: `Test` gets its own automated CI gate, not a manual-only tier. Its trigger shape is different from SIT Gate's, though, so the mechanics need to differ too:

**Proposed shape:** run the gate *after* the deploy, as a second job in the same `deploy-test.yml` run — deploy first (the on-demand action stays fast and simple), then immediately run a lighter P0-only Playwright suite against what was just deployed. The workflow run's overall pass/fail becomes the promotability signal: a green run means this tag is safe to push on to SIT; a red run means it isn't, without blocking the ability to trigger a look in the first place. This intentionally skips the bundle-size/contract-tests/Lighthouse checks SIT Gate also runs — those matter more once something's headed toward Stage/Prod, not for an early single-story look.

How to deploy to a specific environment
---------------------------------------

All five `deploy-*.yml` workflows (`test`, `sit`, `stg`, `uat`, `prod`) already take a `ref` input via `workflow_dispatch` — this proposal changes what value you put there (a tag, not a branch), not the workflow itself. `Dev` stays fully automatic (every merge to `develop`). Tags are cut with `npm version` (built into npm) rather than raw `git tag` — it bumps `package.json`'s version and creates a correctly-formatted **annotated** tag in one step, so nobody has to remember the naming rules or the `-a -m` flags by hand. See Tagging management strategy below for why annotated tags matter.

### 1. Cut a release branch at the end of each sprint

wide4000bash
git checkout develop && git pull
git checkout -b release/v0.1.0
git push -u origin release/v0.1.0

git push origin release/v0.1.0 --follow-tags
gh workflow run deploy-test.yml -f ref=v0.1.0-rc.0

gh workflow run deploy-sit.yml -f ref=v0.1.0-rc.0

# Learning Notes — Release Branches & GitFlow on zimmermann-pwa

**Why this file exists:** I'm FED Lead on this project, Claude-assisted but not Claude-dependent.
When Claude does a piece of analysis for me, the goal isn't just "get the answer" — it's to walk
away understanding the *domain* (GitFlow/release engineering) and the *investigative method* well
enough to reproduce or challenge the answer myself next time. This doc captures both.

**Origin:** the scrum master asked whether zimmermann-pwa's `release/*` branch was already set up
for MRT promotion. That one question turned into a real cross-system investigation. These are my
notes on it, written the day of (2026-08-03), with a verified postscript added later.

---

## Part 1 — The concept: what is a "release branch" actually for?

Before this, I'd have said "a release branch is where you put the code you're about to ship." That's
not wrong, but it's incomplete — the important part is *why it's a separate branch at all* instead of
just deploying straight from `develop`.

**The problem it solves:** `develop` never stops moving — new feature PRs merge into it constantly.
If every environment (Test, SIT, UAT, Stage, Prod) deployed directly from `develop`, none of them
could ever hold still long enough to actually finish testing a specific set of changes — SIT would be
validating build A while build B lands underneath it mid-test.

**The fix:** at a natural boundary (this project uses "end of sprint"), fork a `release/vX.Y.Z`
branch off `develop`. From that point:
- `develop` keeps moving — next sprint's work lands there immediately, unblocked.
- The release branch **freezes scope** — no new features, only critical fixes, and even those go
  through a `fix/release-*` sub-branch, never a direct commit.
- Every environment downstream of Test can now point at *this specific, stable snapshot* instead of
  a moving target.
- When it's finally signed off, it merges to `main` (the "what's actually in prod" branch) **and**
  back to `develop` (so any emergency fixes made on the release branch aren't lost next sprint).

That merge-to-both-branches step is called a **back-merge**, and it's the part of GitFlow most
tutorials gloss over — it's not optional. Skip it and `develop` silently drifts from what's actually
live, and the next release branch inherits a bug that was already fixed once.

**Tags vs. branches — a distinction I hadn't internalized clearly before this:** a branch is a
*moving pointer* (it keeps advancing as commits land). A tag is a *fixed label on one exact commit,
forever*. This project's live tension (see Part 2) is precisely about which of these two things each
environment should actually be pointed at.

---

## Part 2 — How *this* project applies the concept

### The branch table (from `AGENTS.md`)

| Branch | From | Merges to | Who |
|---|---|---|---|
| `feature/*`, `fix/*` | `develop` | `develop` | anyone |
| `release/*` | `develop` | `main` **and** `develop` | squad leads / CI, at sprint close |
| `fix/release-{v}-*` | the release branch | the release branch (then forward via the release's back-merge) | anyone, but only path for code fixes on a release |
| `hotfix/*` | `main` | `main` **and** `develop` | urgent prod-only |

The one nuance I'd have gotten wrong on my own: **you never fix code directly on a release branch.**
Even a squad lead branches a `fix/release-vX.Y.Z-*` sub-branch off it, PRs back into it, and only
*then* does that fix flow to `develop` — automatically, as part of the release's eventual back-merge.
Opening a *second* separate PR straight to `develop` for the same fix would be redundant and is
explicitly disallowed.

### CI can be "wired" without ever having "fired" — this tripped me up initially

The repo's GitHub Actions were already written to key off `release/**` pushes — `digital-sit.yml`
(the full SIT quality gate: Playwright P0, Lighthouse CI, bundle-size, contract tests),
`deploy-sit.yml` (auto-deploys once that gate passes), and `qa.yml`'s cross-browser BrowserStack job
(release PRs only, vs. per-story-scoped on `develop`). My first instinct on seeing all that YAML was
"oh, this must already be in use." **Wrong instinct.** A workflow file existing and being syntactically
wired to a branch pattern tells you nothing about whether that pattern has ever actually existed as a
real branch. I had to separately check:

```bash
gh api repos/ZimmermannAU/zimmermann-pwa/branches --jq '.[].name'   # did release/* ever exist?
git tag -l                                                          # was anything ever tagged?
gh api repos/ZimmermannAU/zimmermann-pwa/rulesets                   # any tag/branch rules?
gh api repos/ZimmermannAU/zimmermann-pwa/branches/release%2Fv0.1.0/protection  # does protection exist?
```

**Lesson:** "the pipeline is configured for X" and "X has happened" are two completely independent
facts. Always check both, and check the second one against the live system, not the YAML.

### A live, unresolved tension: branch-based vs. tag-based promotion

The current documented model (Confluence's Branching Guide) has environments deploy *whatever's
currently on a branch*. There's a **draft, unapproved proposal** sitting on Confluence arguing this
breaks down at scale, for two concrete reasons:

1. PR branches get deleted after merging to `develop` — there's nothing left to point a later deploy
   at, once a story ships.
2. If Test, SIT, and UAT all deploy the *same* release branch as it exists *right now*, they can't run
   independent testing cycles — a fix pushed for UAT is also now sitting on whatever ref SIT hadn't
   finished testing yet.

The proposed fix is standard GitFlow practice this project just hadn't adopted yet: **tag it, and
have every environment deploy an immutable tag, never a moving branch ref.** Each environment can
then sit on a *different* tag simultaneously — decoupled cadences instead of lockstep.

I flagged this to myself as "resolve before cutting the first real release branch," because the two
models use genuinely different tooling (`scripts/tagRelease.sh` vs. `npm version`) — cutting the first
release under one convention and swapping conventions a sprint later is exactly the kind of
inconsistency that becomes tribal knowledge nobody remembers correctly six months on.

---

## Part 3 — The investigative method (the transferable part)

This is the part I want to remember and reapply, independent of this specific question.

**Triangulate three sources that each answer a different question — none of them alone is
trustworthy:**

| Source | What it's actually good for | What it's *not* |
|---|---|---|
| **Codebase** (`gh api`, `git`, grepping workflows/scripts) | Ground truth for what mechanically exists right now — branches, tags, protection rules, CI wiring | Doesn't tell you *why*, or whether it's intentional vs. accidental |
| **Confluence** | Documented process, intent, and decisions-in-progress (the draft proposal, the open checklist) | Can be aspirational — describes what's *supposed* to happen, not necessarily what does |
| **Jira** | Real, live sprint/epic state — what's actually in progress vs. done, with timestamps | Doesn't know anything about git or CI at all |

**The single most useful thing this method surfaced:** the local repo doc
(`.docs/memory/sprintScope.md`) claimed the current sprint was "Sprint 0" with dates that didn't match
reality. The *actual* Jira board showed Sprint 1 had already closed and Sprint 2 was active, with
different boundary dates entirely. If I'd trusted the in-repo doc alone, I'd have told the scrum
master a wrong sprint number. **A doc that lives in the repo is not automatically more current than a
live system it's describing — it's just more convenient to read.** Cross-check anything with a date

# Release Branches — The Simple Version

*(The detailed, deep-dive version of this lives next to this file if I ever need the receipts.
This one's for keeping the idea in my head without wading back through it.)*

## The question that started this

Our scrum master asked: "Is the release branch set up for MRT yet?"

Simple as that sounds, answering it properly meant understanding *what a release branch even is
for*, checking three different places (our code, Confluence, Jira) to make sure I wasn't giving a
half-true answer, and figuring out whether "it doesn't exist" meant "we're behind" or "we're not
there yet, on purpose."

Here's the plain-English version of everything that came out of that.

---

## What's a "release branch," actually?

Picture our codebase as one long, ever-growing document that everyone's editing at once
(`develop`). New paragraphs get added constantly as people finish their bits of work.

Now imagine you need to hand a *stable* copy of that document to a proofreader. You can't hand
them the live document — it'll have changed by the time they finish page one. So instead, you
**print a copy** at a specific moment. That printed copy doesn't change anymore, no matter what
happens to the live document afterward. The proofreader can take their time with it.

That printed copy is the release branch. We "print" (branch off) `develop` at a natural pause
point — for us, that's the end of a sprint — and from then on, that copy is frozen. No new
features get added to it. If something's broken, we fix it directly on that copy, not by trying to
edit the live document and hoping it doesn't clash with everything else moving around it.

Once the proofreader (our test environments — Test, SIT, UAT, Stage) signs off, that frozen copy
becomes what actually goes live, and any typos the proofreader caught get echoed back into the
live document too, so we don't lose them next time we print a new copy.

**That "echoing fixes back" step matters more than it sounds** — skip it, and the live document
quietly starts disagreeing with what's actually out in the world. Next sprint's team re-introduces
a bug that was already fixed, without knowing it.

## Branches vs. tags — one more picture

- A **branch** is a line that keeps growing. Every new commit stretches it further.
- A **tag** is a sticky note stuck to one exact spot on that line. It never moves, even after the
  branch keeps growing past it.

Right now our team documents things in terms of "point the environment at this branch." There's a
sitting proposal (not yet approved) to instead say "point the environment at this exact sticky
note (tag)." The reasoning: a branch keeps moving, so if two environments both point at "the
release branch," they're actually both watching the same live, shifting thing — they can't each
run their own independent test cycle. A tag never moves, so Test can be checking one sticky note
while SIT checks a different, later one, without stepping on each other.

## How our project specifically does this

- Day-to-day work happens on `feature/*` or `fix/*` branches, made from `develop`, merged back
  into `develop`. Normal, no drama.
- A `release/*` branch only gets created by a squad lead (or automation) — not something any
  developer just spins up — and only at the end of a sprint, once there's a stable set of work
  worth freezing.
- If a bug turns up on a release branch, nobody edits it directly. You branch *off* the release
  branch, fix it there, and merge that fix back in. Straightforward — the release branch itself
  stays untouched except through that one door.

## The trap I almost fell into: "it's wired up" ≠ "it's happened"

Our GitHub automation (the CI pipeline) is already written to spring into action the moment a
`release/*` branch shows up — run tests, deploy to SIT, and so on. Seeing all that automation
sitting there ready, my first thought was "oh, this must already be in use somewhere."
